summary:
Martian Map is a web-based Marswalk planning and replay prototype for a 2 × 2 km area near Mount Sharp in Gale Crater. It combines NASA HiRISE imagery and elevation data with derived slope, terrain, and hazard layers, plus a qualitative THEMIS thermal infrared layer. A route planner selects science stops, estimates travel and observation time, and shows where an astronaut could still return to the habitat within the remaining time budget.
Our demonstration visits three targets related to boxwork ridges and nearby terrain. At minute 95, walking speed falls by 20%; a precomputed revised plan drops a lower-priority stop and returns to the habitat. The project helps people explore how scientific value, terrain, and time constraints interact. It is an educational planning prototype based on public data and simplified assumptions, not a system for real astronaut operations.
details:
We built Martian Map as a static, interactive Marswalk planning prototype. The study area is a 2 × 2 km section of Gale Crater near Mount Sharp, represented by a 1,000 × 1,000 grid at 2 m per cell. The map overlays a HiRISE orthorectified image, a HiRISE-derived elevation model, slope and hillshade, automatically derived terrain classes and hazards, and a qualitative daytime THEMIS thermal infrared view.

Users can inspect three science targets, review the planned visit order and route segments, and replay an astronaut’s progress. The map also displays a “safe-return envelope”: at each replay time, the highlighted cells are places from which the astronaut could still return to the habitat before the modeled time limit, after allowing for a reserve. The interface compares the original route with precomputed plans for two disruptions: walking 20% slower and a shortened EVA time budget.

For the current demonstration, the nominal route visits all three targets and returns to the habitat. It is approximately 3.68 km long and takes 196 minutes, including planned observation time. A slowdown at minute 95 causes the revised plan to omit the lower-priority distant observation point. This makes the trade-off between science goals and return time visible.

We processed the terrain and generated route scenarios offline with Python, NumPy, SciPy, and Pillow. The website uses TypeScript, React, Vite, Leaflet, and Apache ECharts. Its static design lets viewers open and replay the prepared scenarios without a server-side planning service.

Our key design choice was to connect the route, schedule, disruption response, and safe-return display through the same terrain-based travel-time model. The terrain classes, hazard thresholds, walking-speed factor, observation durations, and EVA budget are project assumptions. The THEMIS layer is qualitative and does not provide 2 m thermal measurements. The radiation value shown is a background reference, not a real-time reading; location- and season-specific weather data and full life-support constraints are not yet modeled. This prototype must not be used to approve a real EVA.
